findings.title: prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
findings.body: The new code in getClient() calls prisma.credential.update(...) (and the file's other new code references prisma), but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile/runtime error — the Salesforce calendar service will crash (ReferenceError) the first time a client is constructed, breaking all Salesforce integrations.

findings.title: Fake refresh_token literal "refresh_token" is persisted to credentials
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled and the sync endpoint response lacks a refresh_token, the code assigns the literal string "refresh_token" to refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token. Callers (Office365, Zoom, etc.) then spread this into the credential key and write it to the DB via prisma.credential.update. The real refresh token is overwritten with a junk value, so if credential sync is later disabled (or the endpoint changes), the next token refresh will fail permanently and the integration breaks with an invalid_grant. The correct behavior is to preserve the previously stored refresh_token, not fabricate one.

findings.title: Computed zod schema keys are "[object Object]" and effectively meaningless
findings.body: The minimumTokenResponseSchema uses `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the string "[object Object]", so the schema literally defines properties named "[object Object]" rather than "any numeric property is the expiry". In non-strict (strip) zod objects these keys are simply never matched, meaning: (1) no expiry field is validated at all, so callers like Google's refreshAccessToken read token.expiry_date as undefined and write undefined into the credential; (2) the comment's intent is not implemented. Token responses with missing/renamed expiry fields pass validation and corrupt stored credentials.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a fetch Response, breaking axios-based callers that expect .data
findings.body: When sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a `fetch` Response object. But the zoho-bigin (CalendarService.ts line 85-96) and zohocrm (CalendarService.ts line 204-217) callers pass axios-based refresh functions and immediately access `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token`. A fetch Response has no `.data` property, so `tokenInfo.data` is undefined and these usages throw TypeError whenever credential sync is enabled — Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin refresh will crash instead of returning tokens. The abstraction leaks two incompatible response shapes.

findings.title: credentialId passed as userId to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: In refreshAccessToken, the third argument to refreshOAuthTokens is `credentialId` (the credential's DB id) instead of `credential.userId`. When credential sync is enabled, the sync endpoint receives the credential id as `calcomUserId`, so the external app store looks up (or fails to look up) the wrong user entirely and returns tokens for the wrong account — or none.

findings.title: No HTTP method check and unhandled zod parse throws 500s
findings.body: The handler never checks req.method, so GET/PUT etc. are processed; and `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on invalid payloads, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 with a useful message. Similarly JSON.parse of the decrypted payload (line 57) and symmetricDecrypt with an empty key (line 58, since CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY may be unset while APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is truthy only when both vars are set — but empty-string values in .env.example satisfy the check) can throw unhandled errors. Use safeParse, validate the method, and wrap decryption.

findings.title: Decrypted credential keys stored without any schema validation
findings.body: The webhook decrypts the payload and stores `JSON.parse(...)` directly as the credential key with no validation against the app's expected key schema (e.g. googleCredentialSchema). A payload that is valid JSON but missing access_token/refresh_token/expiry, or containing arbitrary extra fields, is persisted verbatim to the user's credential. Since every calendar/video service parses this key with zod on next use, malformed keys break bookings for that user. Validate the decrypted keys against the app's credential schema before writing.

findings.title: Sync request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is unauthenticated and response unchecked
findings.body: The POST to the credential sync endpoint sends only calcomUserId and appSlug with no authentication header (no shared secret), so the receiving side cannot verify the request came from Cal.com — anyone who learns the endpoint URL can request token refreshes for arbitrary users. Additionally, `response.ok` is never checked; a 4xx/5xx (e.g. HTML error page) is returned to the caller and then parsed as a token response, producing confusing failures or corrupting credentials when combined with the relaxed minimumTokenResponseSchema.

findings.title: HubSpot sync response shape mismatch: fetch Response lacks expiresIn/accessToken
findings.body: When sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but the code then reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` and `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` (lines 192, 202), which are undefined on a Response object. `Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` yields NaN, and setAccessToken(undefined) is called — HubSpot requests will be made with an invalid Authorization header. The sync response needs to be `.json()`-ed and mapped to the HubspotToken shape (camelCase) before use.

findings.title: Lark refresh relies on wrapped Response being consumed once
findings.body: When sync is disabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the same fetch Response produced by the inner closure; that's fine. But when sync is enabled, the returned Response is from the sync endpoint and handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp> expects the Lark envelope `{code, data: {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`. A generic sync endpoint returning `{access_token, expires_in}` (as the PR description says: "The response should only contain the access token and expiry date") will fail handleLarkError's code check, and `data.data.refresh_token`/`refresh_expires_date` will be undefined — the stored Lark credential then has a garbage refresh_token and the next refresh deletes the credential. There is no contract alignment between the sync response format and each app's expected token shape.

findings.title: Google sync path writes undefined expiry_date into credential key
findings.body: In the sync path, `res` is a fetch Response whose `.data` is undefined; `const token = res?.data` then makes `token.access_token` and `token.expiry_date` throw (reading property of undefined) or, if the endpoint returns the documented minimal shape without expiry_date, `googleCredentials.expiry_date` becomes undefined. parseRefreshTokenResponse with the relaxed minimum schema (which never validates expiry_date — see separate finding) then persists a credential with expiry_date: undefined. On the next getToken() call, `myGoogleAuth.isTokenExpiring()` will treat undefined expiry as expired, causing a refresh on every single API call and hammering the sync endpoint.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.body: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is typed as the result of `process.env.X && process.env.Y`, i.e. `string | undefined`, not boolean. Truthiness works, but the .env.example ships `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""` — an empty string, which is falsy, so copying the example file as-is silently disables the feature; conversely any non-empty value (e.g. "false") enables it. Export an explicit boolean (e.g. `!!(...)` or compare against "1"/"true") to avoid accidental misconfiguration.

findings.title: Read-then-write credential creation is racy
findings.body: The handler does findFirst then update/create without a transaction or unique constraint. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user+app can both see no existing credential and both create one, resulting in duplicate credentials for the same app/user (the code elsewhere, e.g. office365video/webex/zoom callbacks, has to work around exactly this duplicate-credential problem by deleting extras). Wrap in a transaction or use a unique constraint / upsert semantics.

findings.title: O365 sync path can overwrite refresh_token with the fake "refresh_token" literal
findings.body: In the sync path, parseRefreshTokenResponse applies minimumTokenResponseSchema which does not require refresh_token, then sets it to the literal "refresh_token" if absent. The result is spread into o365AuthCredentials (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and persisted. If the sync endpoint returns only access_token + expiry (as documented), the real Microsoft refresh_token in the stored credential is replaced by the junk literal. Any later refresh without sync enabled (endpoint down, env removed) fails with invalid_grant and the integration is unrecoverable without re-auth. Preserve the existing refresh_token when the response omits one.
